Senator Craig Hickman, Senate Chair Representative Laura Supica, House Chair And members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee
Patti Dubois, Chairperson, Legislative Policy Committee Maine Town and City Clerks' Association Ashley Rand, Vice-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee Maine Town and City Clerks' Association

Re:

LD 1702 - An Act to Election Polling Place Candidate Restrictions

Position:

SUPPORT

The Maine Town & City Clerks' Association is in support of LD 1702 and we thank you for the opportunity to outline our points for your committee.

Members felt that including write-ins in the 250 feet of a voting place prohibiting the influence of voters treats every candidate equally whether their name is listed on the ballot or they are a write-in seeking votes. This helps with candidate confusion and allows for candidate influence rules to be followed by all candidates.

Members also felt that not allowing signatures to be collected at the polls for a future election also clears up confusion for voters. Many voters also get confused and at times frustrated on why someone is campaigning and collecting signatures for the November ballot at a June Election. Prohibiting collecting signatures for a future election and collecting Clean Elections Qualifying Contributions at the polls removes negative public perception of collecting funds on Election Day.

This bill allows for candidate campaigning on Election Day for a current ballot and a future election ballot to be treated equally, removing confusion for voters and candidates running for any Election.

The Maine Town & City Clerks' Association appreciates the opportunity to share its testimony with the Committee. Should any questions arise, please feel free to contact me at (207)6804210 or by email: pdubois@waterville-me.gov .

Testimony in Support of

LD 1702 An Act to Amend Election Polling Place Candidate Restrictions

Dear Senator Hickman, Rep. Supica and Members of Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and
Legal Affairs, I am State Representative Mark Cooper representing District 107, part of
Windham.
I am here to submit this bill LD 1702 An Act to Amend Election Polling Place Candidate
Restrictions in response to a situation that occurred at the June Primary in Windham last year.
On primary day, I was one of 5-6 candidates from the House and Senate Republican AND
Democrat parties that were greeting voters in a space outside the polling location pre-approved
by the Town Clerk and Town Election Warden. It was discovered that an independent or non-
enrolled candidate was allowed to campaign, handout material and collect clean election signatures and contributions inside the polling place alongside other petition gatherers.
The Town Clerk and Election Warden pointed out the "loop hole" that allowed any candidate for
office, not from a recognized party and not on the primary ballot to participate in campaign activities. The current statutes allow any Independent, Un-enrolled party candidate or Write In candidate to legally participate in campaign activities at a Primary Election Polling Place. The
recommendation of the Town Clerk and Election Warden was to amend the current state law to treat all the candidates equally regardless of party or absences of party affiliation. I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

Sincerely,

Mark C. Cooper

10046428:
TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL KEBEDE LD 1702 - Ought Not to Pass

An Act to Amend Election Polling Place Candidate Restrictions

Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs

April 24, 2025

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, good afternoon. My name is Michael Kebede and I am policy director for the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, a statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions through advocacy, education, and litigation. On behalf of our members, I urge you to oppose LD 1702 because it would unconstitutionally restrict core political speech.

Section 3 of LD 1702 would impose content-based restrictions on citizens' rights to free speech. The prohibition in this section would only apply to certain types of speech (collecting or soliciting voter signatures or campaign contributions) and not to others. The specific speech being regulated is core political speech, which includes discussions of candidates, structures and forms of government, the manner in which government is operated or should be operated, and all such matters related to political processes.1

In a case where the U.S. Supreme Court has struck down a restriction on the circulation of electoral petitions in Colorado, the Court explained,

Although a petition circulator may not have to persuade

potential signatories that a particular proposal should prevail to

capture their signatures, he or she will at least have to persuade

them that the matter is one deserving of the public scrutiny and

debate that would attend its consideration by the whole

electorate. This will in almost every case involve an explanation

of the nature of the proposal and why its advocates support it.

Thus, the circulation of a petition involves the type of interactive

communication concerning political change that is appropriately

described

as

"core

political

speech."2

The fact that the restriction proposed in LD 1702 applies to petitions for candidates and not to ballot questions only raises the stakes. That is because "individuals who circulate petitions on behalf of candidates for office

1 Mowles v. Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices, 958 A.2d 897, 902, 2008 ME 160, �� 6-7. 2 Meyer v. Grant, 486 U.S. 414, 421-22 (1988).

typically `must speak to a broader range of political topics' than those who circulate petitions in support of ballot initiatives."3
Though content-based regulations of core political speech are strongly disfavored, they are not universally prohibited. So long as the government has a compelling justification and the restriction is narrowly-tailored to fulfil that justification, and there is no other less-restrictive alternative, the regulation will survive a First Amendment challenge. For example, in Burson v. Freeman, the Supreme Court upheld a Tennessee law that prohibited solicitation of voters and display of campaign material within 100 feet of the entrance to polling places on election day.4 In Burson, the Court observed that the restriction served two compelling interests: protecting the right of citizens to vote freely without undue influence, and ensuring that elections are conducted with integrity.5 It noted that restrictions of the kind enacted by Tennessee were part of a long line of reforms designed to protect voters from race-based intimidation and corruption.6
Maine already has restrictions of this kind in place, and we are not aware of any evidence that they are not sufficiently protective of the right to vote or the integrity of elections. In fact, Maine consistently ranks among the states with the highest voter turnout, and our election laws are a model for states that are interested in expanding the right to vote. If there was evidence that additional laws are needed to ensure that people are able to cast their ballot without undue influence, and free from racial harassment, we would be the first in line to support them. But Section 3 of this bill will, at most, protect voters from minor inconveniences, and that is not a compelling enough reason to impose a content-based restriction on core political speech.

In that case, Illinois argued that the Supreme Court's jurisprudence on ballot question initiative circulators was inapplicable because those cases involved ballot access petitions for initiatives and not candidates. The Seventh Circuit said
This is not a particularly relevant distinction . . . . To the extent it is relevant, it suggests that the burden on the candidates is even greater than that placed on those who circulate petitions for ballot initiatives. For the ballot initiative proponent will generally seek support for the one narrow issue presented in the initiative, while the typical candidate embodies a broad range of political opinions, and thus those who solicit signatures on their behalf must speak to a broader range of political topics.

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Support Of LD 1702 - An Act to Amend Election Polling Place Candidate Restrictions
April 24, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is Rebecca Lambert, and I am providing testimony in support of LD 1702 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). For reference, MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization and aims to help provide policy solutions that work for all residents in Maine and the LPC guides MMA's advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills of municipal interest.
Municipal officials continually support prohibiting or limiting candidate speech at the polls as a way to strengthen the integrity and neutrality of the voting environment. Our members understand that this bill seeks to clearly define a "candidate" which would include write-in candidates, regardless of party affiliation, and reinforces the principle that the voting place should be free from political pressure or influence and that voters have safe environment to cast their ballot.
Thank you for your time and considering our perspective.

Testimony of Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State
And Emily Cook, Deputy Secretary of State
Department of the Secretary of State

April 24, 2025

Testifying in favor of
L.D. 1702 "An Act to Amend Election Polling Place Candidate Restrictions"
Senator Hickman, Representative Supioa and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs, my name is Shemia Bellows, I live in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State. I am testifying in favor of L.D. 1702.
Election Day is for voters. That is the ethos this testimony is based on.
Sections l and 2 do not change current Department interpretation of who is a candidate, or what activities those candidates may engage in within 250 feet of the entrance to the voting place, as well as within the voting place itself. Committee members may recall that in 2024, then-presidential candidate
Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.'s campaign inquired as to whether or not they could collect signatures to get
him on the ballot at the polls on Presidential Primary Day. We instructed the campaign that they could
not, a decision that was upheld by the courts. Having a candidate collect signatures for an office that was on the ballot that day would inevitably result in conversations about which of the various candidates would be the best General Election choice, an inappropriate influence on voters at the polls
that day.
In Section 7, Subsection A seems to be reiterating the same concepts as Sections 1 and 2. We support
Subsection B to keep the immediate vicinity of a voting place free of activities that may give voters pause as to the fairness of elections -- the exchanging of money with a candidate may be worrisome to
some voters. We would just encourage the Committee to ensure that any candidate fundraising or
solicitation is treated equally, whether a candidate is traditionally financed or a Clean Elections candidate. This is impoitant so that Clerks, Wardens and other election officials do not need to spend
time on a busy, high-stress day managing which candidates may or may not be conducting certain
activities in that 250 foot zone.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide this testimony, and I would be happy to answer any questions
that the committee may have.
